title: Snake Atlas
text:
Read the signs
Pain, swelling, puncture marks, bruising, weakness, nausea, or trouble breathing can all be warning signs. Symptoms may change over time, so medical evaluation is important even when the bite looks small.






WarningImportant



This website is educational and is not a substitute for emergency care. Never try to catch or handle the snake. If someone has been bitten, contact emergency services or a poison center now.

title: About the Atlas
text:
The atlas follows a simple path through the snake family tree: Serpentes → family → genus → species. Serpentes is the broad group containing snakes. A family gathers related genera, a genus gathers closely related species, and a species identifies one distinct snake.
The Snake Taxonomy Galaxy begins with Snakes at the center and reveals families, representative genera, and individual species as you select each branch. The Follow This Snake story uses one species as a guide, then expands outward to show its relatives in the same genus.

title: About the Atlas
text: Snakebite Atlas is a small educational website about what to do after a suspected snakebite. It focuses on simple actions that are useful before professional help arrives, without encouraging people to identify or handle a snake.

title: About the Atlas
text:
What guides the information?
The advice follows common first-aid guidance from public-health organizations: prioritize emergency medical care, reduce movement, and avoid harmful home remedies. Local emergency numbers and poison-center services vary by country, so visitors should use the services available where they live.

title: About the Atlas
text:
Why this topic matters
Snakebite envenoming is a neglected public-health problem in many parts of the world. Fast access to appropriate treatment can make a meaningful difference, especially when a person is monitored by trained professionals.

Keep learning
For clinical decisions, use guidance from your local health department, emergency service, or poison center. This page is a starting point for awareness, not a diagnosis tool.

title: About the Atlas
text:
Where the taxonomy comes from
The visualizations use the project dataset in data/snakes-search-results.csv. Each record supplies a scientific species name, an authority, and a Reptile Database link. Family and genus relationships are derived from the scientific name and the site’s taxonomy mapping; species photographs and common names are retrieved from iNaturalist when available.
Because the dataset does not include measurements such as body length, weight, habitat, or geographic range, the supporting comparisons focus on what the data can document directly: the number of records in a family or genus and the relationships between their names.
